texto:
Time-shifted viewing is the watching of a television programme at a time other than its scheduled transmission, usually by playing back a recording or calling up the same episode on demand. The viewer moves the programme; the broadcaster does not. The term exists because television advertising is sold against audiences tied to a broadcast slot, and a growing share of those audiences arrives hours or days later. Measurement companies therefore credit delayed viewing back to the original telecast within fixed windows, and the length of those windows decides how much audience a network can bill for.
How delayed viewing is captured and counted
A meter in a panel home, or tuning data from a set-top box or smart TV, identifies what is on screen by matching an audio code or watermark to a broadcast log. When that content is played back later, the system recognises it as a repeat of an earlier transmission and attributes the viewing to the original programme and its commercials, not to the moment of playback.
In the United States, Nielsen publishes a ladder of data streams. Live counts only viewing at the time of airing. Live plus same day (Live+SD) adds playback until 3am local time. Live+3 and Live+7 extend the window to three and seven days, and Live+35 reaches five weeks after broadcast, according to The Hollywood Reporter's guide to the ratings. The figures that carry money are commercial ratings: C3, the average audience of a programme's commercial minutes counting live viewing plus three days of playback, and C7, which stretches the same measure to seven days. Programme ratings and commercial ratings diverge precisely because time-shifted viewers can fast-forward through the breaks while still watching the show.
On-demand copies of an episode can count as well. Nielsen's Live+3 and Live+7 figures include DVR and on-demand viewing, according to The Hollywood Reporter. In US trading practice, an on-demand episode earns commercial credit only when it carries the same advertising load as the broadcast; a version with different or fewer ads falls outside the commercial rating.
In Britain, Barb, the industry-owned measurement body, uses different labels. Its glossary defines the timeshift audience as the playback audience to a recording of a minute, commercial, daypart or programme. Viewing on the same day as live (VOSDAL) is folded into the overnight file released at 9.30am the next day. The consolidated audience, the sum of live and timeshift viewing within seven days of transmission, is Barb's gold standard and is published eight days after broadcast, according to its frequently asked questions. Since July 2013 Barb has also reported viewing up to 28 days after transmission, outside the gold standard.
Nielsen data for one broadcast drama, published by MediaVillage in December 2016, show how the windows stack: it found that 92 per cent of its five-week audience came within seven days and 8 per cent in days eight to 35. Its commercial audience rose 9 per cent beyond day seven. A cable reality show gained just 4.9 per cent of its viewing after day seven and 5 per cent in commercial audience. Scripted drama keeps accumulating; live sport and news accumulate very little.
On the sell side, networks negotiate which window a deal guarantees and owe make-goods if it is missed. On the buy side, agency investment groups decide which stream to accept as currency. Pay-TV distributors and device makers, through recording and ad-skipping features, shape how many commercials survive the delay.
From the VCR to the cloud recorder
The legal basis came first. Universal City Studios and Walt Disney Productions sued Sony in 1976 over the Betamax video recorder. On January 17, 1984, the US Supreme Court ruled 5-4 for Sony, with Justice John Paul Stevens writing that private, noncommercial time-shifting in the home was fair use. Copying a whole programme, the Court said, "does not have its ordinary effect of militating against a finding of fair use", according to the US Copyright Office's summary of the case. The phrase entered the industry's vocabulary from there.
Digital recording made the practice routine. TiVo shipped the first consumer digital video recorder (DVR) on March 31, 1999, and BSkyB launched Sky+, a satellite set-top box with a built-in recorder, in Britain in September 2001. Nielsen began reporting DVR playback in the last week of December 2005, splitting results into live, Live+SD and Live+7, according to a BetaNews report from December 23, 2005. Sara Erichson, then general manager of Nielsen's national services, called it "a major milestone in ratings history".
Commercial ratings followed. Nielsen launched them on May 31, 2007, after months of negotiation with clients, according to WARC, and C3 became the default currency of the US upfront market. The window was a compromise: long enough to credit recorded viewing, short enough that advertisers with dated messages, such as film releases, were not paying for audiences reached after the event.
The window then crept outward. Remote storage won a legal green light when the Second Circuit ruled on August 4, 2008, that Cablevision's network DVR did not infringe copyright, opening the way to recordings held on operators' servers rather than in the home. In June 2014 Fox and CBS confirmed preliminary deals with a major agency to trade on C7, which MediaPost reported was GroupM, a buyer then handling an estimated 25 to 30 per cent of US television spend. Fox stopped releasing Live+SD data in November 2015, and ABC followed in November 2019. Karey Burke, then president of ABC Entertainment, explained the change in a staff memo: "People used to plan their lives around television, now they plan television around their lives."
Why buyers and sellers argue about windows
For marketers, the window is a price lever. Longer windows add audience to the same commercial, so a C7 guarantee is easier for a network to meet than a C3 guarantee, and fewer make-goods are owed when a show underperforms live. Buyers counter that delayed audiences are worth less: they skip more ads, they see time-sensitive messages too late, and they arrive after the campaign's flighting has moved on. Nielsen data cited by WARC in October 2007 found that up to one in five DVR viewers of the most popular US programmes skipped or fast-forwarded through the commercials.
The scale has moved over time. Nielsen's third-quarter 2015 Total Audience Report put US adult time-shifted viewing at 48 minutes a day, with DVRs in 49 per cent of TV households. In Britain, recorded playback averaged 20 minutes a day in 2025, against 90 minutes of live broadcast viewing, according to Ofcom's Media Nations 2026 report as summarised by informitv in July 2026. Both fell from the year before, live viewing by 12 minutes and playback by two.
PPC Land's coverage of US measurement shows the concept still sets the boundaries of the market. Nielsen's Gauge, the monthly share-of-viewing report, counts linear viewing on a Live+7 basis, so a recorded broadcast episode watched four days later is classed as linear rather than streaming.
Limitations and disputes
Crediting playback to the original broadcast hides when the audience actually watched. Longer windows also delay the numbers: Barb's gold standard arrives eight days after transmission, and a 35-day rating is five weeks old before a programme's audience is fully known.
Ad avoidance remains the central dispute. When Dish Network launched AutoHop in May 2012, a feature that skipped whole commercial breaks in recorded prime-time shows, Fox sued on May 24, 2012. The Ninth Circuit upheld the denial of a preliminary injunction on July 24, 2013. Under a settlement reported in February 2016, AutoHop works on Fox programmes only seven days after transmission, which is to say after the C7 window closes.
Buyers have never fully accepted extended windows. When the C7 deals were reported in 2014, John Muszynski, chief investment officer of Starcom MediaVest Group's Spark unit, wrote: "C7? Did someone really agree to pay for C7 in a buyers market?" Local television is a further gap. In January 2018 the 4A's and the Television Bureau of Advertising (TVB) asked Nielsen to replace its local Live Only stream with Live+1, arguing that Live Only misses delayed spot audiences. Steve Lanzano, TVB's president, said Live+1 was "now the best representation of the spot TV audience".
What time-shifted viewing is not
On-demand streaming. Watching an original series on a subscription service has no broadcast to shift from. Catch-up players such as broadcaster video on demand (BVOD) services were built as catch-up products, but their viewing counts as time-shifted only when it is matched to the broadcast version with the same ads.
Linear TV. Linear television is the scheduled stream itself. Time-shifted viewing is a way of consuming linear content later, and the industry still books it as linear.
Timeshift channels. A "+1" channel retransmits a schedule an hour late. Viewers watching it are watching a separate live channel, not shifting a programme themselves.
Recent developments
The US currency itself has changed underneath the windows. Nielsen's Big Data + Panel method, combining a panel of about 42,000 homes with set-top box and smart TV data, became the standard currency for the 2025 upfront, and seven further methodology changes took effect on August 31, 2026. Neither announcement altered the C3 and C7 windows.
Storage limits, once a brake on delayed viewing, are disappearing in the cloud. YouTube TV's Sports Plan, announced on December 10, 2025, includes unlimited DVR storage. Meanwhile the British figures point the other way: recorded playback is shrinking as viewers move to on-demand services that sit outside the timeshift definition altogether.
Timeline
- 1976: Universal City Studios and Walt Disney Productions sue Sony over the Betamax recorder.
- January 17, 1984: US Supreme Court rules 5-4 in Sony Corp. of America v. Universal City Studios that home time-shifting is fair use.
- March 31, 1999: TiVo ships the first consumer DVR.
- September 2001: BSkyB launches the Sky+ recorder in Britain.
- December 2005: Nielsen begins reporting DVR playback in Live+SD and Live+7 data streams.
- May 31, 2007: Nielsen launches commercial ratings; C3 becomes the main US trading currency.
- October 2007: Nielsen data show up to one in five DVR viewers of top programmes skip ads.
- August 4, 2008: Second Circuit rules Cablevision's remote-storage DVR does not infringe copyright.
- May 24, 2012: Fox sues Dish Network over the AutoHop ad-skipping feature.
- July 2013: Barb begins reporting viewing up to 28 days after broadcast.
- July 24, 2013: Ninth Circuit upholds denial of Fox's preliminary injunction against AutoHop.
- June 2014: Fox and CBS confirm preliminary C7 deals with a major agency.
- November 2015: Fox stops releasing Live+SD data.
- February 2016: Fox and Dish settle; AutoHop limited to seven days after transmission on Fox programmes.
- December 2016: Nielsen publishes analysis of commercial audiences beyond seven days.
- January 2018: 4A's and TVB ask Nielsen to replace local Live Only data with Live+1.
- November 2019: ABC stops releasing Live+SD data.
- September 2025: Nielsen Big Data + Panel becomes the standard US currency.
- December 10, 2025: YouTube TV announces genre plans, with unlimited DVR storage in its Sports Plan.
- July 2026: Ofcom reports UK recorded playback fell to 20 minutes a day in 2025.
- August 31, 2026: Nielsen deploys seven changes to its Big Data + Panel currency.

Summary
Who. Viewers create time-shifted audiences by recording or replaying programmes. Nielsen in the United States and Barb in Britain measure them; networks, agencies and advertisers trade on them; pay-TV distributors and device makers supply the recorders and set their features.
What. Viewing of a broadcast programme after its scheduled airtime, credited back to the original telecast within fixed windows: Live+SD, Live+3, Live+7 and Live+35 in US programme ratings, C3 and C7 in US commercial ratings, and 7-day consolidated and 28-day figures at Barb.
When. The legal basis dates from the Supreme Court's Betamax ruling of January 17, 1984. Measurement of digital recording began in December 2005, and C3 trading in May 2007. Barb added 28-day data in July 2013.
Where. In every television market with recording devices or matched on-demand services, with the most developed trading rules in the United States and Britain.
Why. Broadcasters want credit for audiences who no longer watch on schedule. Advertisers want to pay only for viewers who see their commercials in time. The window length is where those two interests meet, and where most of the disputes happen.
